t: You fell asleep in a Walmart. When you woke up, everyone was gone. Not just from the store,
from everywhere. And you'd be stuck in here for the next year. You stopped in after work for a few
things, sat down in one of the display recliners to check your phone, and closed your eyes for a
second. When you open them, it's three in the morning. The lights are still on, the music is
still playing. But there's nobody here. No workers, no cleaning crew, nothing. The front
doors are locked. Your phone has no signal. You figure you'll just wait for the morning shift.
Then you walk past electronics. Every TV on the wall is showing the same message.
Stay indoors. Do not travel. Further instructions will follow. They never do.
Day one. When the sun comes up, the parking lot is full of cars with nobody in them.
The city is quiet. No sirens, no traffic, no planes. The morning shift never comes.
So you do the math. Around 4,000 cans of food. 2,000 bottles of water in the back. Bags of rice,
beans, pasta, peanut butter. If you're smart about it, one person could live off this store
for years. The problem is, you have no idea what's happening outside. And you have no idea who else
is still out there. That first night, you don't sleep much. You make a bed behind the customer
service counter where nobody can see you from the doors. It's the quietest place in the store.
Too quiet. Around midnight, a car alarm goes off somewhere outside. It goes for almost a minute.
Then it just stops. Not like someone turned it off. Like the battery died. Later, you hear dogs
barking far away. A lot of them. Then nothing. You lie there staring at the ceiling, telling
yourself someone's going to come. The army, the police, anyone. In the morning, you'll hear sirens
and this will all be over. You don't hear sirens. Not the next morning. And not any morning after that.
Day three. First rule. Stay away from the glass. You stack shopping carts against the front doors
and drag shelves in front of them. Anyone walking by can see right into this place.
You move to the back of the store. The camping aisle has everything you need.
A tent, a sleeping bag, lanterns, and enough batteries to last a long time. From here,
you can hear the whole store, but nobody outside can see you. Day five. In electronics, you find a
hand crank emergency radio. No batteries needed. You crank it for two minutes and start scanning.
Static. Static. More static. Then, right at the end of the dial, a voice. A woman reading a list
of numbers, slow and calm. Fourteen. Nine. Twenty-two. Six. Over and over. You have no idea what they
mean, but it's the first human voice you've heard in five days and you sit there listening
to it for an hour. The next night, you turn it on again. Same station, same numbers. On day 11,
she stops in the middle of a number and she never comes back on. Day seven. For one week,
it's honestly not bad. You eat whatever you want, you ride scooters down the aisles,
you play every game in electronics, you sleep on a different mattress every night. But at night,
the store gets really quiet. And that's when you start to realize how alone you actually are.
Day 10. You find a whiteboard in the back office and write down rules.
Real rules. The kind you don't break, even when you're tired.
Rule 1. Never open the front doors. Rule 2. No lights near the front of the store after dark.
Rule 3. Count the food every Sunday. Rule 4. Always know where your flashlight is.
Rule 5. If you hear something, you don't go looking for it. You wait.
It feels a little crazy writing rules for yourself in an empty store. But without them,
every day starts to feel the same. And you've already caught yourself talking out loud to
nobody. The rules keep you sharp. Later on, Rule 5 is the one you'll wish you followed.
Day 14. The fresh food goes first. Bananas turn black. The bread grows mold.
The smell from the produce section gets so bad, you stop walking past it.
You make a new rule. Eat the stuff that spoils first. Save the cans for later.
Day 30. The lights die. The music stops. The freezers stop humming.
For the first time, the store is completely silent.
The hardware section has two generators and some gas cans from the lawn and garden area.
But gas runs out. So you only run the generator for one thing.
A light at night. Everything else, you do in the dark.
Day 38. In the back of the stock room,
there's a ladder bolted to the wall that goes up to a hatch in the roof.
You've been scared to use it. Today, you climb.
It's the first fresh air you've had in over a month.
And the view is worse than you thought. The whole city is dark.
Highways full of cars that aren't moving.
Smoke still rising from three different spots downtown.
You set up buckets and a tarp to catch rainwater, just in case.
And right before you head back down, you notice something.
Way across the city, on top of a tall building, one light is blinking.
On and off. On and off. Someone else is out there.
You just don't know if that's a good thing.
Day 45. Without power, every freezer in the store starts to rot.
Hundreds of pounds of meat and ice cream, all going bad at once.
You wrap the whole section in plastic and tape it shut.
You don't go back there again.
Day 52. You're moving a shelf in the dark when it slips.
A piece of broken glass from a freezer door slices right across your hand.
It's deep. Deeper than any cut you've ever had.
And there's no hospital. No doctor. Nobody coming.
You wrap it in a shirt and run to the pharmacy with the flashlight in your teeth.
A bottle of pills you read the label on three times before you take one.
For four days, your hand is swollen and hot.
You barely sleep. You start to think this is how it ends.
On day 56, the swelling goes down. You add a new rule to the whiteboard.
In here, small mistakes are big ones.
Day 60. By now, you have a routine.
Check the doors. Count the food.
Work out. Mark another day on the wall.
It's the only thing that keeps the days from blending together.
You drink three bottles of water a day.
At that rate, the water lasts almost two years.
Food isn't the problem anymore. Being alone is.
Day 75. The storm starts in the afternoon.
By night, the wind is so loud it sounds like the whole building is breathing.
Then you hear a crack above aisle 12.
Part of the roof gives way and the rain pours straight in.
You run with buckets, tarps, anything you can find.
But it's too much. Water spreads across the floor,
under the shelves, into the bottom rows of food. It goes all night.
In the morning, you count what's left. 600 cans are ruined.
Labels peeled off, cans dented, boxes turned to mush.
600. For the first time, the math doesn't feel safe.
This store isn't going to last forever. And neither are you, if you stay here forever.
Day 90. You see something you haven't seen in three months.
Flashlights. Out in the parking lot.
Three of them. Walking between the cars, checking everyone.
You turn off your lantern and don't move.
One of them walks up to the front doors and pulls on the handle.
The carts shake, but they hold. After a few minutes, they leave.
Day 100. You find a box of cake mix, a pan, and the camping stove.
It takes three tries, but you make something that looks almost like a cake.
You stick one candle in the middle. It's not your birthday. It's just day 100.
But it feels like it should mean something.
So you sit on the floor of the bakery aisle and sing to yourself.
Quietly, so nobody outside can hear.
You think about the people you haven't seen in a hundred days.
Whether any of them are out there, sitting somewhere just like this.
You blow out the candle. You don't make a wish.
Day 120. You count the food like you always do.
And something's off. You're short six cans of soup.
You count again. Still six short.
Then you check the stock room.
There are footprints in the dust, and they're not yours.
The doors are still blocked. Nothing outside got in,
which means whoever made these footprints was already inside.
If someone is in the store with you, you want to know where.
So you set traps. Not to hurt anybody. Just to hear them.
You tie bells from the toy aisle onto fishing line and string them across the stock room doors.
You pour a thin line of flour across the back hallway so footprints will show.
Then you grab every baby monitor in the baby aisle.
Eight of them. You hide them all over the store
and keep the receivers lined up next to your tent.
For two weeks, nothing. Just a quiet hiss.
Then, on night 15, one of the monitors picks something up.
You check which monitor it is. It's the one in the stock room.
You've spent weeks trying to figure out where they're hiding.

You climb up and push a tile out of the way.
There's a blanket up there. Empty soup cans.
